subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What is half - life of a reaction ? Illustrate your answer with an example.

verification.note: Unit 4 (Chemical Kinetics) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.73-76, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. The printed definition and the printed ¹⁴C example are both CORRECT and are kept. The half life symbol is written t1/2 in plain text throughout this unit. NOTE: the printed answer stops at the definition and the number 5730 years. The added sentence, that a first order half life does not depend on the starting amount, is the property the example actually illustrates, and it is the line VSAQ 8 and LAQ 1 are marked on.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The half life of a reaction, written t1/2, is
the time in which the concentration of a
reactant falls to one half of its initial
It is a measure of how fast a reaction is:
a short half life means a fast reaction.
steps.why: The half life is useful because it is one number that does not need the starting concentration to be quoted with it. For a first order reaction it depends only on k, so two samples of different size have the same half life.
common_mistakes: Saying it is the time for half the reaction to finish in every case. The definition is about the concentration of a reactant falling to half.
Writing that a long half life means a fast reaction. It is the opposite: a long half life means a slow reaction.
steps.memory_tip: Half life = time for the reactant to drop to half. Short half life, fast reaction.
steps.margin_note: The words one half of its initial concentration carry this mark.

steps.label: The example
lines: Example: the decay of ¹⁴C has
In 5730 years half of the ¹⁴C present at the
start is left. In another 5730 years half of
that is left, that is one quarter.
so the half life does not depend on how
much was there to begin with.
steps.why: Following the sample through two half lives is what shows the meaning: a fixed fraction is lost in each equal interval, not a fixed amount. That is the shape of first order decay, and it is why the formula contains only k.
common_mistakes: Writing that all the ¹⁴C is gone after two half lives. After two half lives one quarter is still left.
Saying a bigger sample has a longer half life. For first order the half life is 0.693/k whatever the starting amount.
steps.memory_tip: Half, then half of that. One half life takes a sample to 1/2, two take it to 1/4.
steps.margin_note: One worked example plus t1/2 = 0.693/k completes this mark.

insider_note: Follow the example through a second half life. Writing that a quarter is left after 11460 years is the line that shows the definition was understood rather than copied.
